title: Determinant-open coordinates for the unit scheme of a finite algebra
statement:
Let $k$ be a field [def-weil-field], let $A$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional commutative $k$-algebra [def-weil-pbc-algebra-hom-quotient, def-weil-finite-dimensional-subspace], and let $e_1,\ldots,e_d$ be a $k$-basis of $A$, with $d\geq1$. Write $e_i e_j=\sum_{h=1}^d c_{hij}e_h$ with $c_{hij}\in k$. In the polynomial algebra $B=k[x_1,\ldots,x_d]$ [def-weil-pbc-mv-polynomial-ring], set
$$M(x)_{hj}=\sum_{i=1}^d c_{hij}x_i,\qquad N(x)=\det M(x)\in B,$$
with determinant as in [def-weil-pbc-matrix-determinant]. Let $U=D(N)\subseteq\operatorname{Spec}B=\mathbb A^d_k$ be the open subscheme whose points are the prime ideals not containing $N$ [def-weil-affine-spectrum, def-sbc-affine-space, def-weil-open-immersion]. For every commutative $k$-algebra $R$, evaluation identifies
$$U(R)=\{(a_1,\ldots,a_d)\in R^d:N(a_1,\ldots,a_d)\in R^\times\},$$
and the rule $(a_i)\mapsto\sum_i e_i\otimes a_i$ is a bijection $U(R)\simeq(A\otimes_kR)^\times$, natural in $R$ [lem-weil-pbc-algebra-tensor-pushout-universal-property]. Here $B'^\times$ denotes elements with multiplicative inverses in the commutative ring $B'$, and $X(R)=\operatorname{Hom}_k(\operatorname{Spec}R,X)$. If $P$ is any affine $k$-scheme with natural bijections $P(R)\simeq(A\otimes_kR)^\times$ for all commutative $k$-algebras $R$, these bijections induce a $k$-scheme isomorphism $U\simeq P$. Finally, if $1_A=\sum_i b_i e_i$ with $b_i\in k$, then $N(b_1,\ldots,b_d)=1$, so $U$ is nonempty. No separability or reducedness assumption on $A$, and no reducedness assumption on $R$, is imposed.

source.place: Proposition 12.60, proof, printed p.250: basis coordinates and norm polynomial. The identical multiplication-matrix construction applies to any finite-dimensional commutative algebra. For arbitrary test algebras R, read norm invertible, rather than merely nonzero (see report Source error).

proof.text: Put $D=B[1/N]$. By [lem-weil-pbc-affine-open-section-vanishing-prime](b), $U=D(N)$ is affine with coordinate ring $D$, and its inclusion corresponds to $B\to D$. By [def-weil-affine-spectrum] and the polynomial universal property [def-weil-pbc-mv-polynomial-ring], morphisms $\operatorname{Spec}R\to\operatorname{Spec}B$ over $k$ are evaluations $x_i\mapsto a_i$. The localization definition [def-weil-ring-localization-away] makes $N/1$ a unit of $D$; hence a map $D\to R$ restricts to an evaluation with $N(a)$ a unit. Conversely, [lem-weil-pbc-localization-away-universal-property] extends every such evaluation uniquely to $D\to R$. The extension respects $k$ because its restriction on $B$ does. This proves exactly the asserted description of $U(R)$, including the zero test ring.

source.place: Proposition 12.60, proof, printed p.250; multiplication-matrix generalization to a finite commutative algebra, with unit in place of nonzero for arbitrary test algebras

proof.text: Fix a commutative $k$-algebra $R$. By [lem-weil-pbc-free-module-base-change-free], $(e_i\otimes1)_{i=1}^d$ is an $R$-basis of $A\otimes_kR$. Thus $a\mapsto u(a)=\sum_i e_i\otimes a_i$ is a bijection from $R^d$ to its underlying module. The tensor multiplication formula [lem-weil-pbc-algebra-tensor-pushout-universal-property](1) gives $u(a)(e_j\otimes1)=\sum_h(e_h\otimes1)(\sum_i c_{hij}a_i)$. Hence multiplication by $u(a)$ has matrix $T=M(a)$. In the Leibniz determinant formula [def-weil-pbc-matrix-determinant], evaluation commutes with every finite sum and product and with the signs. Therefore $\det T=N(a)$.

source.place: Proposition 12.60, proof, printed p.250; multiplication-matrix generalization to a finite commutative algebra, with unit in place of nonzero for arbitrary test algebras

proof.text: If $u(a)$ has inverse $v$, the matrices of multiplication by $u(a)$ and $v$ in the basis of step 2 are two-sided inverses: their products act identically on each basis vector. Apply [lem-weil-pbc-matrix-left-inverse-minors](2) with $n=m=d$, matrix $T$, scalar $f=1$ and this inverse matrix. The unique maximal minor of a square matrix is $\det T$, so $1\in(\det T)$; thus $\det T$ is a unit. Conversely, if $\det T$ is a unit, [lem-weil-pbc-matrix-adjugate-identity] makes $(\det T)^{-1}\operatorname{adj}(T)$ an inverse matrix. Apply this inverse to the coordinate vector of $1\otimes1$, obtaining an element $v$ with $u(a)v=1$. Commutativity gives $vu(a)=1$ as well. Consequently $u(a)$ is a unit exactly when $N(a)$ is a unit. Restricting the bijection in step 2 to these subsets, and using step 1, proves $U(R)\simeq(A\otimes_kR)^\times$; the inverse of a unit is unique, so using unit elements or units with their inverses gives the same set.

source.place: Tags 07DQ (lemma-matrix-left-inverse), square case of (2), and 080R (lemma-matrix-right-inverse), adjugate identity in its proof

proof.text: For a $k$-algebra homomorphism $\varphi:R\to R\prime$, the induced tensor map sends $e_i\otimes a_i$ to $e_i\otimes\varphi(a_i)$; its existence and uniqueness follow by applying [lem-weil-pbc-algebra-tensor-pushout-universal-property](2),(3) to the two maps $A\to A\otimes_kR\prime$ and $R\to A\otimes_kR\prime$. It sends a unit and its inverse to mutually inverse elements. On coordinates it sends $a$ to $(\varphi(a_i))$, and $N(\varphi(a_i))=\varphi(N(a_i))$ by the finite-sum formula of step 2. On $U(R)$ the extension maps commute with $\varphi$ by their uniqueness in step 1. Therefore both directions of the restricted coordinate bijection commute with every $\varphi$, proving naturality without any assumption that $R$ is reduced.

source.place: Proposition 12.60, proof, printed p.250; multiplication-matrix generalization to a finite commutative algebra, with unit in place of nonzero for arbitrary test algebras

proof.text: Let $P$ be as in the statement and put $C=\Gamma(P,\mathcal O_P)$, with its structural $k$-algebra map. Since $P$ and $U$ are affine, [def-weil-affine-spectrum] identifies their $R$-points with $\operatorname{Hom}_{k\text{-alg}}(C,R)$ and $\operatorname{Hom}_{k\text{-alg}}(D,R)$ respectively. The requirement that a scheme map be over $k$ is exactly that its corresponding ring map commute with the two structural maps from $k$, by contravariant functoriality of $\operatorname{Spec}$. Composing the natural bijection of steps 1--4 with the inverse of the given bijection for $P$ gives natural bijections $\Phi_R:\operatorname{Hom}_{k\text{-alg}}(D,R)\to\operatorname{Hom}_{k\text{-alg}}(C,R)$. Apply [lem-weil-pbc-coyoneda-iso-of-natural-hom-bijection] in the category of commutative $k$-algebras: $\theta=\Phi_D(\mathrm{id}_D):C\to D$ is an isomorphism inducing these very bijections. Its spectrum is the required $k$-scheme isomorphism $U\simeq P$. This uses only affine test schemes, not a Yoneda assertion on all schemes.

source.place: Proposition 12.60, proof, printed p.250; multiplication-matrix generalization to a finite commutative algebra, with unit in place of nonzero for arbitrary test algebras

proof.text: For the coordinates $b_i$ of $1_A$, the $j$th column of $M(b)$ is the coordinate vector of $(\sum_i b_i e_i)e_j=e_j$. Uniqueness of basis expansions gives $M(b)=I_d$. In the determinant formula [def-weil-pbc-matrix-determinant], the identity permutation contributes $1$ and every other permutation contributes $0$, so $N(b)=1$. Step 1 with $R=k$ yields a $k$-point of $U$. The source $\operatorname{Spec}k$ has a point by [def-weil-affine-spectrum], so this morphism exhibits a point of $U$, proving nonemptiness. All arguments used only freeness and commutativity; nilpotents in $A$ or $R$ do not affect them.
